One-page summaryScore, rank, domains, and goals on one page.

Northern Kentucky’s economy is usually reported as part of the Cincinnati metro, which hides how Boone, Kenton, and Campbell counties are doing on their own. This index measures the three counties together against metros of 250,000+ residents, across the nation or within the region, giving funders, partners, and policymakers one consistent picture of where the region leads, where it lags, and whether it is moving in the right direction.

What this dashboard does

Use the to see every metro at once, to line Northern Kentucky up against any peer, or to go the other way and map the region from the inside, by county, census tract, or city, across housing, income, commuting, and who lives where.

Want to see how Northern Kentucky scores on the Prosperity Index?

See the region’s overall 0 to 10 score, how it ranks against 196 U.S. metros, and its score on each of the 30 metrics.

      Goals

      BE NKY Growth Partnership has identified these eight goals as the priorities where progress by 2030 will do the most to raise prosperity for Northern Kentucky residents and strengthen the region’s competitiveness with metros across the country. Together they cover growth, wages and income, workforce participation, entrepreneurship, high-value industries, talent, and affordability.

      Each goal is a value to reach by 2030, tracked against a straight path from 2019.

      How goals are tracked
      • GRP per capita is the region’s GDP divided by its population, in current dollars.
      • Every goal is a set value chosen by the Partnership.
      • Dollar goals are in current dollars, so part of the progress toward them will come from inflation.
      • The path runs in a straight line from the 2019 value to the goal in 2030. On track means the latest value is at or ahead of the path, allowing a small margin. Met means the goal value is already reached.

                About the small-area data
                • Prosperity Index metrics appear in the county view with the same values and years used on the Regional Metrics page. Most of the rest are American Community Survey five-year estimates for 2020 to 2024. Jobs by industry are annual average covered employment from the BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages for 2024, summed across private and public ownership, with each sector's establishment count in its description. Census tracts average about 4,000 residents; cities and towns are incorporated cities plus census-designated places, so unincorporated areas appear only in the tract view.
                • Where a measure is a share, the counts behind it are shown with the percentage, so 72.6% homeownership also reads as the number of owner-occupied homes out of all occupied homes. Measures the index expresses per 1,000 residents are shown here as plain counts instead, since rates per 1,000 earn their keep when comparing Northern Kentucky with other metros rather than when comparing its own counties. A few sector cells are withheld by the BLS to protect individual employers; those read as no data, and a sector whose total includes a withheld ownership class is a lower bound.
                • CTC credentials are not shown here. Gateway Community and Technical College reports to the federal data system at a single Florence address even though it runs campuses in Boone and Kenton, so any county split of its output says more about mailing addresses than about where people earn credentials.
                • Small areas carry wide margins of error. The ± figure beside each value is the 90 percent margin of error; differences smaller than the margins may not be real. Tracts dominated by institutions (a university, a jail) can look unusual on employment and income measures. Several measures describe an area without being good or bad, such as median age or the share of homes that are single-family; for those the dashboard reports the gap with the region and makes no judgment.
                • Fourteen of the sixteen metrics are built from the same tables and formulas as the regional metric. Poverty and unemployment are ACS estimates here, while the regional pages use SAIPE and BLS LAUS, so the regional figures differ slightly.
                • Index metrics drawn from establishment data, BEA accounts, or patent filings (GRP, pay, job growth, business applications, patents, advanced industries, childcare, amenity jobs, parks, credentials) are not published below the county level and appear only in the county view.
                • Better and worse are only claimed where the gap between an area and the region is wider than the two margins of error combined. Where it is not, the dashboard says there is no clear gap.
                How the scores work
                • Each metric is converted to a z-score against the benchmark metros (lower-is-better metrics are flipped), capped at ±3. Dollar and skewed metrics use a log scale.
                • Domain scores average their metric z-scores and are re-standardized; the overall score averages all metric z-scores and needs at least 5 of 6 domains.
                • Metric scores place each metric’s z-score on a bell curve and scale it to 0 to 10, so a small difference in value moves the score only a little, even where many metros are bunched together. Domain and overall scores are the share of benchmark metros a region outperforms, times 10. Northern Kentucky is scored against the metros but is not part of the benchmark, since its counties sit inside the Cincinnati metro.
                • Choose the benchmark on the Overview or from the menu beside the page tabs. United States compares Northern Kentucky with all 196 metros of 250,000+ residents. Middle America uses the Census Bureau's Midwest (Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, and Wisconsin) plus Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and West Virginia: 55 metros. A metro counts toward a state when its principal city is there. In both indexes every score, rank, and median is recalculated within the group, so the same value can score differently in each.
                • Index scores use 2024, the latest year with data for every metric. Metrics that already have 2025 values show them on the Regional Metrics page as raw data, but they are not scored until every metric reaches 2025. Each year from 2015 to 2024 re-scores every region on that year's data. Ranks count all regions, including Northern Kentucky, so a rank of 43rd of 197 means 42 regions score higher. Regions are built from member counties (2023 OMB delineations).
                Source: BE NKY Growth Partnership. Data from the Census Bureau, BEA, BLS, USPTO PatentsView, NCES IPEDS, and County Health Rankings & Roadmaps. Data through 2025; index scored on 2024. Inside NKY adds small-area measures from the 2020 to 2024 ACS five-year estimates, on 2024 Census cartographic boundaries. Dashboard updated October 2026.
